claim: QLIPP provides simultaneous measurement of density, anisotropy, and orientation of structures in unlabeled live cells and tissue slices.
source: We report quantitative label-free imaging with phase and polarization (QLIPP) for simultaneous measurement of density, anisotropy, and orientation of structures in unlabeled live cells and tissue slices.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a primary finding of the work.

claim: QLIPP combined with deep neural networks can predict fluorescence images of diverse cell and tissue structures.
source: We combine QLIPP with deep neural networks to predict fluorescence images of diverse cell and tissue structures.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the manuscript with experimental data.

claim: QLIPP images reveal anatomical regions and axon tract orientation in prenatal human brain tissue sections that are not visible using brightfield imaging.
source: QLIPP images reveal anatomical regions and axon tract orientation in prenatal human brain tissue sections that are not visible using brightfield imaging.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by comparative images in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Multi-channel 2.5D U-Net enables computationally efficient prediction of fluorescence images in three dimensions and over large fields of view.
source: We report a variant of U-Net architecture, multi-channel 2.5D U-Net, for computationally efficient prediction of fluorescence images in three dimensions and over large fields of view.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated with performance comparisons in Tables 1-4.

claim: Data normalization methods enable accurate prediction of myelin distribution over large brain regions.
source: Further, we develop data normalization methods for accurate prediction of myelin distribution over large brain regions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Experimental defects in labeling human tissue can be rescued with quantitative label-free imaging and neural network models.
source: We show that experimental defects in labeling the human tissue can be rescued with quantitative label-free imaging and neural network model.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 7A and 7D with cyan arrowheads indicating rescued artifacts.

claim: Fluorescence imaging combined with deep learning has opened new avenues for understanding complex biological processes.
source: Combination of fluorescence imaging and automated analysis of image content with deep learning (Moen et al., 2019; Belthangady and Royer, 2019; Van Valen et al., 2016) has opened new avenues for understanding complex biological processes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Labeling cytoskeletal polymers often perturbs their native assembly kinetics.
source: For example, labeling cytoskeletal polymers often perturbs their native assembly kinetics (Belin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Belin et al., 2014.

claim: Genetic labeling of human tissue and non-model organisms is not straightforward and the labeling efficiency is often low.
source: Genetic labeling of human tissue and non-model organisms is not straightforward and the labeling efficiency is often low.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Label-free imaging requires minimal sample preparation as it measures the sample's intrinsic properties.
source: By contrast, label-free imaging requires minimal sample preparation as it measures the sample's intrinsic properties.
evidence: This is stated as a fundamental property of label-free imaging.

claim: Label-free imaging is capable of visualizing many biological structures simultaneously with minimal photo-toxicity and no photo-bleaching.
source: Lable-free imaging is capable of visualizing many biological structures simultaneously with minimal photo-toxicity and no photo-bleaching, making it particularly suitable for live-cell imaging.
evidence: This is stated as a known advantage of label-free imaging.

claim: Classical label-free microscopy techniques such as phase contrast, DIC, and polarized light microscopy are qualitative.
source: Classical label-free microscopy techniques such as phase contrast (Zernike, 1955), differential interference contrast (DIC) (Nomarski, 1955), and polarized light microscopy (Schmidt, 1926; Inoue, 1953) are qualitative.
evidence: This is stated with citations to the original methods.

claim: Quantitative phase imaging measures optical path length, which reports density of the dry mass.
source: Quantitative phase imaging (Popescu et al., 2006; Waller et al., 2010; Tian and Waller, 2015) measures optical path length, that is, specimen phase, which reports density of the dry mass (Barer, 1952).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on quantitative phase imaging and the relationship to dry mass.

claim: Quantitative polarization microscopy in transmission mode reports angular anisotropy of the optical path length (retardance) and axis of anisotropy (orientation) without label.
source: Quantitative polarization microscopy in transmission mode reports angular anisotropy of the optical path length, that is, retardance, (Inoue, 1953; Oldenbourg and Mei, 1995; Mehta et al., 2013) and axis of anisotropy, that is, orientation, without label.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on quantitative polarization microscopy.

claim: Quantitative phase microscopy has been used to analyze membrane mechanics, density of organelles, cell migration, and fast propagation of action potential.
source: For example, Quantitative phase microscopy (Park et al., 2018) has been used to analyze membrane mechanics, density of organelles (Imai et al., 2017), cell migration, and recently fast propagation of action potential (Ling et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific applications of quantitative phase microscopy.

claim: Quantitative polarization microscopy enabled discovery of the dynamic microtubule spindle.
source: Similarly, quantitative polarization microscopy has enabled discovery of the dynamic microtubule spindle (Inoue, 1953; Keefe et al., 2003), analysis of retrograde flow of F-actin network (Oldenbourg et al., 2000), imaging of white matter in adult human brain tissue slices (Axer et al., 2011a; Axer et al., 2011b; Menzel et al., 2017; Mollink et al., 2017; Zeineh et al., 2017; Henssen et al., 2019), and imaging of activity-dependent structural changes in brain tissue (Koike-Tani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original discovery and subsequent applications.

claim: Current methods for joint imaging of density and anisotropy are limited in throughput due to complexity of acquisition or can only be used for 2D imaging due to the lack of accurate 3D image formation models.
source: However, current methods for joint imaging of density and anisotropy are limited in throughput due to complexity of acquisition or can only be used for 2D imaging due to the lack of accurate 3D image formation models.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of prior methods that motivates the current work.

claim: Deep learning has enabled translation of qualitative and quantitative phase images into fluorescence images.
source: Recently, deep learning has enabled translation of qualitative and quantitative phase images into fluorescence images (Ounkomol et al., 2018; Christiansen et al., 2018; Rivenson et al., 2018a; Rivenson et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2019; Petersen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work on image translation using deep learning.

claim: U-Net has been widely applied to image segmentation and translation tasks.
source: Among different neural network architecture, U-Net has been widely applied to image segmentation and translation tasks (Ronneberger et al., 2015; Milletari et al., 2016; Ounkomol et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original U-Net paper and applications.

claim: U-Net's success arises primarily from its ability to exploit image features at multiple spatial scales and its use of skip connections between encoding and decoding blocks.
source: U-Net's success arises primarily from its ability to exploit image features at multiple spatial scales, and its use of skip connections between the encoding and decoding blocks.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for U-Net's effectiveness based on its architecture.

claim: The accuracy of predicting molecular structures from label-free data depends on the dynamic range and consistency of contrast in the label-free data.
source: The accuracy with which the molecular structure can be predicted depends not just on the model, but also on the dynamic range and the consistency of the contrast with which the structure is seen in the label-free data.
evidence: This is stated as a principle for image translation accuracy.

claim: Some anisotropic structures are not visible in phase imaging data and therefore cannot be learned from phase imaging data.
source: Some of the anisotropic structures are not visible in phase imaging data and therefore cannot be learned from phase imaging data.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of using only phase imaging for prediction.

claim: Reported methods of image translation have not utilized optical anisotropy.
source: Reported methods of image translation have not utilized optical anisotropy, which reports important structures such as cell membrane and axon bundles.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in prior work that the current study addresses.

claim: Volumetric prediction using 3D U-Net is computationally expensive, requiring downsampling at the expense of spatial resolution.
source: Furthermore, previous work has mostly demonstrated prediction of single 2D fields of view. Volumetric prediction using 3D U-Net has been reported, but it is computationally expensive, such that downsampling the data at the expense of spatial resolution is required (Ounkomol et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work demonstrating the computational limitation.

claim: QLIPP combines quantitative polarization microscopy with the concept of phase from defocus.
source: QLIPP combines quantitative polarization microscopy (Oldenbourg and Mei, 1995; Shribak and Oldenbourg, 2003; Mehta et al., 2013) with the concept of phase from defocus (Streibl, 1984; Waller et al., 2010; Streibl, 1985; Noda et al., 1990; Claus et al., 2015; Jenkins and Gaylord, 2015a; Jenkins and Gaylord, 2015b; Soto et al., 2017), to establish a novel method for volumetric measurement of phase, retardance, and orientation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1A, with citations to the underlying methods.

claim: QLIPP's optical path is simpler relative to earlier methods.
source: QLIPP's optical path is simpler relative to earlier methods (Shribak et al., 2008), reconstruction algorithms are more accurate, and reconstruction software is open-source.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of QLIPP compared to prior methods, with a citation.

claim: QLIPP can be implemented on existing microscopes as a module and can be easily multiplexed with fluorescence.
source: QLIPP can be implemented on existing microscopes as a module and can be easily multiplexed with fluorescence.
evidence: This is stated as a practical advantage of the method.

claim: Label-free measurement of anisotropy allowed visualization of axon orientations across whole sections of human brain tissue.
source: Label-free measurement of anisotropy allowed us to visualize axon orientations across whole sections.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: QLIPP data increases accuracy of prediction of myelination in developing human brain compared to brightfield data.
source: We demonstrate that QLIPP data increases accuracy of prediction of myelination in developing human brain as compared to brighfield data.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative comparisons in Table 4 and Figure 7.

claim: Label-free measurements are more robust to experimental variations in labeling than fluorescent staining.
source: Finally, we demonstrate robustness of the label-free measurements to experimental variations in labeling, which leads to more consistent prediction of myelination than possible with the experimental staining.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 7A and 7D.

claim: QLIPP is a transmission polarization microscope based on computer controlled liquid crystal universal polarizer.
source: The light path of QLIPP is shown in Figure 1A. It is a transmission polarization microscope based on computer controlled liquid crystal universal polarizer (Oldenbourg and Mei, 1995; Shribak and Oldenbourg, 2003; Mehta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1A, with citations to the underlying technology.

claim: In QLIPP, specimens are illuminated with five elliptical polarization states for sensitive detection of specimens' retardance.
source: In QLIPP, specimens are illuminated with five elliptical polarization states for sensitive detection of specimens' retardance (Shribak and Oldenbourg, 2003; Mehta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to the method.

claim: Variations in the density of the specimen cause changes in refractive index and distort the wavefront of the incident light.
source: Variations in the density of the specimen, for example lower density of nuclei relative to the cytoplasm, cause changes in refractive index and distort the wavefront of the incident light.
evidence: This is stated as a physical principle underlying phase imaging.

claim: Anisotropic variations in specimens' density result from alignment of molecules along a preferential axis.
source: Anisotropic variations in the specimens' density result from alignment of molecules along a preferential axis, for example lipid membrane has higher anisotropy relative to the cytoplasm due to the alignment of lipid molecules.
evidence: This is stated as a physical principle underlying retardance imaging.

claim: QLIPP uses Stokes vector representation of partially polarized light to model the transformation from specimens' optical properties to acquired intensities.
source: First, we utilize Stokes vector representation of partially polarized light (Born and Wolf, 2013; Bass et al., 2009; Azzam, 2016) to model the transformation from specimens' optical properties to acquired intensities (Equation 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to the formalism.

claim: QLIPP reconstructs 3D volumes of retardance, slow-axis orientation, brightfield, and degree of polarization.
source: By inverting this transformation, we reconstruct 3D volumes of retardance, slow-axis orientation, brightfield, and degree of polarization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as the output of the reconstruction algorithm.

claim: A two-step background correction method is used to correct non-uniform background polarization.
source: We use a two-step background correction method (Materials and methods) to correct the non-uniform background polarization (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: QLIPP enables reconstruction of brightfield and degree of polarization, in contrast to previous work that reconstructs just retardance and slow-axis orientation.
source: In addition to retardance and slow-axis orientation, our use of Stokes formalism enables reconstruction of brightfield and degree of polarization, in contrast to previous work that reconstructs just retardance and slow-axis orientation (Shribak and Oldenbourg, 2003; Mehta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as an advantage over prior methods, with citations.

claim: QLIPP uses phase transfer function formalism to model how 3D phase information is transformed into brightfield contrast.
source: Second, we utilize phase transfer function formalism (Streibl, 1985; Noda et al., 1990; Claus et al., 2015; Jenkins and Gaylord, 2015a; Jenkins and Gaylord, 2015b; Soto et al., 2017) to model how 3D phase information is transformed into brightfield contrast (Equation 17).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to the formalism.

claim: Phase reconstruction from brightfield volume shows nucleoli in positive contrast relative to background consistently as the nucleoli move through the focus.
source: Phase reconstruction from the brightfield volume shows nucleoli in positive contrast relative to background consistently as the nucleoli move through the focus (Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 2—video 1.

claim: The two-step background correction is essential for background-free retardance and orientation images, but not for phase image.
source: We note that the two-step background correction is essential for background-free retardance and orientation images, but not for phase image (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In dividing U2OS cells, the phase image shows three-dimensional dynamics of dense cellular organelles such as lipid vesicles, nucleoli, and chromosomes.
source: In the dividing U2OS cell (Figure 2—video 2, Figure 2—video 3), the phase image shows three-dimensional dynamics of dense cellular organelles, such as lipid vesicles, nucleoli, and chromosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 2—video 2 and Figure 2—video 3.

claim: Retardance and slow-axis orientation in U2OS cells show dynamics of membrane boundaries, spindle, and lipid droplets.
source: The retardance and slow-axis orientation in U2OS cells (Figure 2—video 2, Figure 2—video 3) show dynamics of membrane boundaries, spindle, and lipid droplets.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 2—video 2 and Figure 2—video 3.

claim: Phase images identify cell bodies and axon tracts in mouse and developing human brain tissue sections because of variations in their density.
source: At larger spatial scale, the phase image identifies cell bodies and axon tracts in mouse and developing human brain tissue sections because of variations in their density.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Density variations are more visible and interpretable in phase image compared to brightfield image.
source: These density variations are more visible and interpretable in phase image as compared to the brightfield image (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Axon tracts appear with noticeably high contrast in retardance and orientation images of mouse and human brain slices.
source: Axon tracts appear with noticeably high contrast in retardance and orientation images of mouse and human brain slices (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: The high retardance of axons arises primarily from myelin sheath that has higher density perpendicular to the axon axis.
source: The high retardance of the axons arises primarily from myelin sheath that has higher density perpendicular to the axon axis (de Campos Vidal et al., 1980; Menzel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work on the optical properties of myelin.

claim: The slow axis of axon tracts is perpendicular to the orientation of the tracts.
source: Therefore, the slow axis of the axon tracts is perpendicular to the orientation of the tracts.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the myelin structure.

claim: In stitched retardance and orientation images of a whole mouse brain slice, not only white matter tracts but also orientation of axons in cortical regions is visible.
source: Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 5 show stitched retardance and orientation images of a whole mouse brain slice, in which not only the white matter tracts, but also orientation of axons in cortical regions is visible.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 5.

claim: The degree of polarization decreases when the specimen exhibits multiple scattering and increases when the specimen exhibits diattenuation.
source: The DOP decreases when the specimen exhibits multiple scattering and increases when the specimen exhibits diattenutation, that is, polarization-dependent absorption.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 caption as a property of the degree of polarization measurement.

claim: Retardance measures single scattering events within the specimen that alter the polarization of light but do not reduce the degree of polarization.
source: The difference between retardance and degree of polarization is that retardance measures single scattering events within the specimen that alter the polarization of the light, but do not reduce the degree of polarization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a distinction between the two measurements.

claim: Low degree of polarization indicates multiple scattering events that reduce the polarization of light and mismatch of specimen optical properties from model assumptions.
source: On the other hand, low degree of polarization indicates multiple scattering events that reduce the polarization of light and thus mismatch of the specimen optical properties from the model assumptions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the degree of polarization measurement.

claim: The Python software for QLIPP reconstruction is available at https://github.com/mehta-lab/reconstruct-order.
source: The Python software for QLIPP reconstruction is available at https://github.com/mehta-lab/reconstruct-order.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a resource availability statement.

claim: The optimization of neural network models led to a residual 2.5D U-Net that translates a small stack of label-free channels to the central slice of fluorescent channel throughout 3D volume.
source: The optimization led us to a residual 2.5D U-Net that translates a small stack (5–7 slices) of label-free channels to the central slice of fluorescent channel throughout 3D volume.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as the outcome of model optimization.

claim: Mouse kidney tissue section was chosen as a test dataset because it has both anisotropic and isotropic structures (F-actin and nuclei).
source: We chose the mouse kidney tissue section because it has both anisotropic and isotropic structures (F-actin and nuclei).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as the rationale for choosing this dataset.

claim: Both F-actin and nuclei structures in mouse kidney tissue are robustly labeled with no noticeable artifacts.
source: Additionally, both structures are robustly labeled with no noticeable artifacts.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an advantage of the mouse kidney dataset.

claim: Ounkomol et al., 2018 showed fluorescence predicted by 3D U-Net is superior to 2D U-Net.
source: Our work builds upon earlier work (Ounkomol et al., 2018) on predicting fluorescence stacks from brightfield stacks using 3D U-Net. Ounkomol et al., 2018 showed fluorescence predicted by 3D U-Net is superior than 2D U-Net.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Applying 3D U-Net to microscopy images poses limitations because typical microscopy stacks are bigger in their extent in the focal plane and smaller in extent along the optical axis.
source: However, applying 3D U-Net to microscopy images poses a few limitations. Typical microscopy stacks are bigger in their extent in the focal plane (∼2000 × 2000 pixels) and smaller in extent along the optical axis (usually <40 Z slices).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of 3D U-Net for microscopy data.

claim: The use of 3D translation models often requires upsampling of the data in Z, which increases data size and makes training computationally expensive.
source: Therefore, the use of 3D translation models often requires upsampling of the data in Z, which increases data size and makes training 3D translation model computationally expensive.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the data structure limitation.

claim: In mouse kidney tissue, the retardance image highlights capillaries within glomeruli and brush borders in convoluted tubules.
source: In mouse kidney tissue, the retardance image highlights capillaries within glomeruli, and brush borders in convoluted tubules, among other components of the tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: Nuclei appear in darker contrast in the retardance image because of the isotropic architecture of chromatin.
source: The nuclei appear in darker contrast in the retardance image, because of the isotropic architecture of chromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an explanation for the observed contrast.

claim: Three model architectures were evaluated: slice→slice (2D), stack→slice (2.5D), and stack→stack (3D).
source: We evaluated three model architectures to predict fluorescence volumes: slice→slice (2D in short) models that predict 2D fluorescence slices from corresponding 2D label-free slices, stack→slice (2.5D in short) models that predict the central 2D fluorescence slice from a stack of adjacent label-free slices, and stack→stack (3D in short) models that predict 3D fluorescent stacks from label-free stacks.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as the experimental design.

claim: For 2.5D models, 3D translation is achieved by predicting one 2D fluorescence plane per stack of label-free inputs.
source: For 2.5D models, 3D translation is achieved by predicting one 2D fluorescence plane per stack (z = 3, 5, 7) of label-free inputs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as the approach for 2.5D models.

claim: A residual connection was added between the input and output of each block to speed up model training.
source: We added a residual connection between the input and output of each block to speed up model training (Milletari et al., 2016; Drozdzal et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior work on residual connections.

claim: To fit 3D models on the GPU, overlapping sub-stacks were predicted and stitched together to get the whole 3D stack.
source: In order to fit 3D models on the GPU, we needed to predict overlapping sub-stacks, which were stitched together to get the whole 3D stack ( see Materials and methods and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for the description of the network architecture and training process).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a practical implementation detail.

claim: Pearson correlation coefficient and structural similarity index (SSIM) were used to evaluate the performance of the models.
source: We used Pearson correlation coefficient and structural similarity index (SSIM) (Wang and Bovik, 2009) between predicted fluorescent stacks and target fluorescent stacks to evaluate the performance of the models (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to the SSIM method.

claim: Predictions with 2D models show discontinuity artifacts along the depth.
source: The predictions with 2D models show discontinuity artifacts along the depth (Figure 3, Figure 3—video 2), as also observed in prior work (Ounkomol et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 3 and Figure 3—video 2, with a citation to prior work.

claim: The 3D model predicts smoother structures along the Z dimension with improved prediction in the XY plane.
source: The 3D model predicts smoother structures along the Z dimension with improved prediction in the XY plane.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: 2.5D model shows prediction accuracy comparable to 3D model, with higher prediction accuracy as the number of z-slices in the 2.5D model input increases.
source: 2.5D model shows prediction accuracy comparable to 3D model, with higher prediction accuracy as the number of z-slices in the 2.5D model input increases. (Figure 3C and D; Table 1; Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3C and D, Table 1, and Figure 3—video 2.

claim: The 2.5D model could be trained with approximately 3× more parameters than 3D model in shorter time.
source: While 2.5D model shows similar performance to 3D model, we note that we could train the 2.5D model with ∼3× more parameters than 3D model (Materials and methods) in shorter time.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an advantage of the 2.5D model.

claim: Training a 3D model with 1.5M parameters required 3.2 days, training a 2D model with 2M parameters required 6 hr, and training a 2.5D model with 4.8M parameters and five input z-slices required 2 days, using approximately 100 training volumes.
source: In our experiments, training a 3D model with 1.5M parameters required 3.2 days, training a 2D model with 2M parameters required 6 hr, and training a 2.5D model with 4.8M parameters and five input z-slices required 2 days, using ∼100 training volumes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison of training times.

claim: The large memory usage of 3D model significantly limits its training batch size and thus the training speed.
source: This is because the large memory usage of 3D model significantly limits its training batch size and thus the training speed.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an explanation for the longer training time of 3D models.

claim: The Python code for training image translation models is available at https://github.com/czbiohub/microDL.
source: The Python code for training our variants of image translation models is available at https://github.com/czbiohub/microDL.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a resource availability statement.

claim: When multiple label-free measurements are jointly used as inputs, both F-actin and nuclei are predicted with higher fidelity compared to when only a single label-free measurement is used as the input.
source: We found that when multiple label-free measurements are jointly used as inputs, both F-actin and nuclei are predicted with higher fidelity compared to when only a single label-free measurement is used as the input (Table 2 and Table 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 2 and Table 3.

claim: The continuity of prediction along Z-axis improves as more label-free contrasts are used for prediction.
source: The continuity of prediction along Z-axis improves as more label-free contrasts are used for prediction (Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 4—video 1.

claim: Using complementary label-free contrasts boosts the performance of 2.5D models to exceed the performance of 3D single-channel models without significantly increasing the computation cost.
source: We note that using complementary label-free contrasts boosts the performance of 2.5D models to exceed the performance of 3D single-channel models without significantly increasing the computation cost (compare Table 1 and Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by comparing Table 1 and Table 2.

claim: Fine F-actin bundles can be predicted from multiple label-free inputs when the model is trained to minimize the difference between the fluorescence target and prediction over only the foreground pixels in the image.
source: We found fine F-actin bundles can be predicted from multiple label-free inputs when the model is trained to minimize the difference between the fluorescence target and prediction over only the foreground pixels in the image (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: When only a single contrast is provided as input, a model trained on phase images has higher prediction accuracy than the model trained on brightfield images.
source: Interestingly, when only a single contrast is provided as the input, a model trained on phase images has higher prediction accuracy than the model trained on brightfield images.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: Phase image has consistent, quantitative contrast along z-axis, while the depth-dependent contrast in brightfield images makes the translation task more challenging.
source: This is possibly because the phase image has consistent, quantitative contrast along z-axis, while the depth-dependent contrast in brightfield images makes the translation task more challenging.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a possible explanation for the observation.

claim: The improvement of using phase over brightfield images is not observed when retardance and orientation are also included as inputs.
source: This improvement of using phase over brightfield images, however, is not observed when the retardance and orientation are also included as inputs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: Quantitative retardance and orientation complement the qualitative brightfield input and simplify the translation task.
source: This is possibly because quantitative retardance and orientation complement the qualitative brightfield input and simplify the translation task.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a possible explanation for the observation.

claim: 2.5D multi-contrast models predict 3D structures with superior accuracy than single channel 3D U-Net models.
source: In conclusion, above results show that 2.5D multi-contrast models predict 3D structures with superior accuracy than single channel 3D U-Net models, but have multiple practical advantages that facilitate scaling of the approach.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the model comparison experiments.

claim: Structures of varying density and order can be learned with higher accuracy when complementary physical properties are combined as inputs.
source: In addition, the results show that structures of varying density and order can be learned with higher accuracy when complementary physical properties are combined as inputs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the experiments.

claim: QLIPP's high-resolution, quantitative nature, sensitivity to low anisotropy of gray matter, and throughput make it attractive for imaging the architecture and activity in brain slices.
source: QLIPP's high-resolution, quantitative nature, sensitivity to low anisotropy of gray matter (Figure 2), and throughput make it attractive for imaging the architecture and activity in brain slices.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an advantage of QLIPP for brain imaging.

claim: Six cortical layers are distinguishable in terms of strength of the retardance signal and the orientational pattern in adult mouse brain.
source: We also found that six cortical layers are distinguishable in terms of strength of the retardance signal and the orientational pattern.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: Layer I of mouse cortex contains axon bundles parallel to the cortical layer.
source: These data are consistent with reports that layer I contains axon bundles parallel to the cortical layer (Zilles et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work on cortical anatomy.

claim: Layer VI of mouse cortex contains axon bundles that feed to and from the corpus callosum, so the orientation of the axon is not as orthogonal to the cortical layers as the axons in the other layers.
source: Layer VI contains axon bundles that feed to and from the corpus callosum, so the orientation of the axon is not as orthogonal to the cortical layers as the axons in the other layers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: Layers IV and V of mouse cortex contain higher density of cell bodies and correspondingly lower density of axons, leading to lower signal in retardance.
source: Layers IV and V contain higher density of cell bodies and correspondingly lower density of the axons, leading to lower signal in retardance.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: Gestational week 24 and week 20 correspond to the earliest stages of oligodendrocyte maturation and early myelination in the cerebral cortex.
source: We next imaged brain sections from developing human samples of two different ages, gestational week 24 (GW 24) (Figure 6A–C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and GW20 (Figure 6D–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) which correspond to the earliest stages of oligodendrocyte maturation and early myelination in the cerebral cortex (Jakovcevski et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2012; Snaidero and Simons, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work on brain development.

claim: The retardance in subplate is higher than cortical plates at both GW24 and GW20 time points.
source: The retardance in subplate is higher than cortical plates at both time points, which is consistent with the reduced myelin density in the cortical plate relative to the white matter.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: QLIPP has the sensitivity to detect axon orientation in the developing cortical plate, despite the lower retardance in developing brain compared to adult brain due to low myelination in early brain development.
source: Importantly, with our calibration and background correction procedures (Materials and methods), our imaging approach has the sensitivity to detect axon orientation in the developing cortical plate, despite the lower retardance in developing brain compared to adult brain due to the low myelination in early brain development (Miller et al., 2012; Snaidero and Simons, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior work on brain development.

claim: Different cortical layers are visible in the retardance and orientation images at both GW24 and GW20 time points.
source: Different cortical layers are visible in the retardance and orientation images at both time points.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: Different anatomical structures in the developing human brain can be identified without additional stains by referencing to the developing human brain atlas.
source: With this approach, we could identify different anatomical structures in the developing human brain without additional stains by referencing to the developing human brain atlas (Bayer and Altman, 2003, Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to the brain atlas.

claim: Individual axon tracts are visible in phase image while with lower contrast as the phase image measures the density variation but not the axon orientation.
source: The individual axon tracts are also visible in phase image while with lower contrast as the phase image measures the density variation but not the axon orientation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: The above data are the first report of label-free imaging of architecture and axon tract orientation in prenatal brain tissue.
source: To our knowledge, the above data are the first report of label-free imaging of architecture and axon tract orientation in prenatal brain tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a claim of novelty.

claim: The ability to resolve axon orientation in the cortical plate of the developing brain demonstrates the sensitivity and resolution of QLIPP.
source: The ability to resolve axon orientation in the cortical plate of the developing brain, which exhibits very low retardance, demonstrates the sensitivity and resolution of our approach.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion about the method's capabilities.

claim: The human brain undergoes rapid myelination during late development as measured with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
source: The human brain undergoes rapid myelination during late development as measured with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Heath et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work on brain development.

claim: Interpretation of myelination from MRI contrast requires establishing its correlation with histological measurements of myelin levels.
source: Interpretation of the myelination from MRI contrast requires establishing its correlation with histological measurements of myelin levels (Khodanovich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work on MRI validation.

claim: QLIPP data indicate that label-free measurements are predictive of the level of myelination but relationship among them is complex.
source: QLIPP data in Figure 6 indicate that label-free measurements are predictive of the level of myelination but relationship among them is complex (Figure 7C and F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 7C and F.

claim: A data normalization and training strategy was developed that enables prediction of myelination across large slices and multiple developmental time points.
source: Importantly, we developed a data normalization and training strategy that enables prediction of myelination across large slices and multiple developmental time points.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological contribution.

claim: A properly trained model can rescue inconsistencies in fluorescent labeling of myelin.
source: We also found that a properly trained model can rescue inconsistencies in fluorescent labeling of myelin, which is often used as histological groundtruth.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 7.

claim: FluoroMyelin is a lipophilic dye that can stain myelin without permeabilization.
source: In order to train the model, we measured the level of myelination with FluoroMyelin, a lipophilic dye that can stain myelin without permeabilization (Monsma and Brown, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the dye's properties.

claim: Detergents used in most permeabilization protocols remove myelin from the tissue and affect label-free measurements.
source: We found the detergents used in most permeabilization protocols remove myelin from the tissue and affect our label-free measurements.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an experimental observation.

claim: To avoid overfitting and build a model that generalizes to different developmental ages and different types of sections of the brain, imaging datasets from GW20 and GW24 with two different brain sections for each age were pooled.
source: To avoid overfitting and build a model that generalizes to different developmental ages and different types of sections of the brain, we pooled imaging datasets from GW20 and GW24 with two different brain sections for each age.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a training strategy.

claim: The prediction accuracy improves as more label-free contrasts are included in training for human brain tissue.
source: Similar to the observations in the mouse kidney tissue, the prediction accuracy improves as more label-free contrasts are included in training but with higher accuracy gain compared to the mouse kidney tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 4.

claim: The additional information provided by adding more label-free channels is more informative for the model to predict the more complex and variable human brain structures.
source: This is most likely because the additional information provided by adding more label-free channels is more informative for the model to predict the more complex and variable of human brain structures.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an explanation for the observation.

claim: 2.5D model with all four input channels shows similar performance as 2D model for human brain tissue dataset due to the relatively large depth of field compared to the sample thickness.
source: On the other hand, 2.5D model with all four input channels shows similar performance as 2D model for this dataset due to the relatively large depth of field (∼16 μm) compared to the sample thickness (12 μm thick), so additional Z-slices only provide phase information but no extra structural information along the z dimension. (Table 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 4.

claim: FluoroMyelin was predicted using label-free images of whole sections from GW24 and GW20 brains that were not used for model training or validation.
source: To test the accuracy of prediction over large human brain slices that span multiple fields of view, we predicted FluoroMyelin using label-free images of whole sections from GW24 and GW20 brains that were not used for model training or validation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as the experimental design for testing.

claim: Model inference was run on each field of view and then stitched together to obtain a stitched prediction with 20,000 × 20,000 pixels.
source: We ran model inference on each field of view and then stitched the predicted images together to obtain a stitched prediction with 20,000 × 20,000 pixels (Figure 7A and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 7A and D.

claim: The stitched predictions are the largest predicted fluorescence images of tissue sections that have been generated.
source: To the best of our knowledge, these are the largest predicted fluorescence image of tissue sections that have been generated.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a claim of novelty.

claim: Myelination level was predicted in sections from both GW24 and GW20 time points with a single model.
source: We were able to predict myelination level in sections from both time points with a single model, with increasing accuracy as we included more label-free channels as the input, similar to our observations from the test dataset of the mouse kidney slice (Table 4 and Figure 7B and E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 4 and Figure 7B and E.

claim: Model-predicted FluoroMyelin intensities correlate with the target FluoroMyelin stain significantly better than the label-free contrasts alone.
source: The scatter plots of pixel intensities show that model-predicted FluoroMyelin intensities correlate with the target FluoroMyelin stain significantly better than the label-free contrasts alone (Figure 7C and Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 7C and Figure 7F.

claim: While label-free contrasts are predictive of FluoroMyelin stain, the complex relations between them makes estimation of myelin level from label-free contrasts challenging.
source: This illustrates the value of predicting fluorescence from label-free contrasts: while the label-free contrasts are predictive of FluoroMyelin stain, the complex relations between them makes estimation of myelin level from label-free contrasts challenging.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The neural network can learn the complex transformation from label-free contrasts to FluoroMyelin stain and enables reliable estimation of myelin levels.
source: The neural network can learn the complex transformation from label-free contrasts to FluoroMyelin stain and enables reliable estimation of myelin levels.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion about the method's capabilities.

claim: Per-image normalization commonly applied to image segmentation tasks did not preserve the intensity variation across images and led to artifacts in prediction.
source: We found that per-image normalization commonly applied to image segmentation tasks did not preserve the intensity variation across images and led to artifacts in prediction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an experimental observation.

claim: Numbers of background pixels vary across images and can bias the normalization parameters if not excluded from normalization.
source: The two main issues that need to be accounted for in image translation tasks are: (1) numbers of background pixels vary across images and can bias the normalization parameters if not excluded from normalization (Yang et al., 2019), and (2) there are batch variations in the staining and imaging process when pooling multiple datasets together for training.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work on normalization issues.

claim: There are batch variations in the staining and imaging process when pooling multiple datasets together for training.
source: The two main issues that need to be accounted for in image translation tasks are: (1) numbers of background pixels vary across images and can bias the normalization parameters if not excluded from normalization (Yang et al., 2019), and (2) there are batch variations in the staining and imaging process when pooling multiple datasets together for training.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a challenge in image translation.

claim: Batch variation is less pronounced in quantitative label-free imaging but remains quite significant in fluorescence images of stained samples.
source: While batch variation is less pronounced in quantitative label-free imaging, it remains quite significant in fluorescence images of stained samples and therefore needs to be corrected.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation about the data.

claim: Normalizing per-dataset with the median of inter-quartile range of foreground pixel intensities gives the most accurate intensity prediction.
source: We found that normalizing per-dataset with the median of inter-quartile range of foreground pixel intensities gives the most accurate intensity prediction (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 2D model with phase, retardance, and orientation as input has correlation and similarity scores close to the best 2.5D model but training takes just 3.7 hr to converge, while the best 2.5D model takes 64.7 hr to converge.
source: Notably, the 2D model with phase, retardance, and orientation as the input has correlation and similarity scores close to the best 2.5D model but the training takes just 3.7 hr to converge, while the best 2.5D model takes 64.7 hr to converge (Table 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 4.

claim: The 2D phase reconstruction captures the density variation encoded in the brightfield Z-stack that is informative for the model to predict axon tracts accurately.
source: This is likely because the 2D phase reconstruction captures the density variation encoded in the brightfield Z-stack that is informative for the model to predict axon tracts accurately.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an explanation for the observation.

claim: FluoroMyelin stain intensity faded unevenly over time and formed dark patches in the images, possibly due to quenching of FluoroMyelin by the antifade chemical in the mounting media.
source: For example, we found FluoroMyelin stain intensity faded unevenly over time and formed dark patches in the images (indicated by cyan arrow heads in Figure 7A and D), possibly due to quenching of FluoroMyelin by the antifade chemical in the mounting media.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 7A and D.

claim: Quenching of dye does not affect the physical properties measured by the label-free channels.
source: However, this quenching of dye does not affect the physical properties measured by the label-free channels.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an advantage of label-free imaging.

claim: The model trained on images without artifacts predicted the expected staining pattern even with the failure of experimental stain.
source: Therefore, the model trained on images without artifacts predicted the expected staining pattern even with the failure of experimental stain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a demonstration of robustness.

claim: The robustness of predicted fluorescence to experimental variations is particularly valuable for precious tissue specimens such as archival prenatal human brain tissue.
source: This robustness is particularly valuable for precious tissue specimens such as archival prenatal human brain tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an implication of the findings.

claim: QLIPP is designed to be easy to adopt and multiplex with fluorescence microscopy.
source: We have designed QLIPP to be easy to adopt and multiplex with fluorescence microscopy.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a design principle.

claim: Using QLIPP requires a single liquid-crystal polarization modulator and a motorized Z stage.
source: Using QLIPP requires a single liquid-crystal polarization modulator and a motorized Z stage.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a practical requirement.

claim: The open-source Python software for QLIPP is free to use for non-profit research.
source: Our open-source Python software is free to use for non-profit research.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a resource availability statement.

claim: Shribak reported joint imaging of 2D phase and retardance with OI-DIC and OI-POL, which required six polarization modulators and acquisition protocol more complex than QLIPP.
source: Shribak (Shribak et al., 2008) has reported joint imaging of 2D phase and retardance with orientation-independent differential interference contrast (OI-DIC) and orientation-independent PolScope (OI-POL), which required six polarization modulators and acquisition protocol more complex than QLIPP.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to prior work.

claim: Ptychography-based phase retrieval method has been extended with polarization sensitive components for joint imaging of 2D phase and retardance, albeit requiring hundreds of images.
source: Ptychography-based phase retrieval method has been extended with polarization sensitive components for joint imaging of 2D phase and retardance (Ferrand et al., 2018; Baroni et al., 2020), albeit requiring hundreds of images.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior work.

claim: QLIPP uses one polarization modulator, compared to six used by OI-DIC, and fewer images (5 × number of Z slices), compared to hundreds in ptychography-based method, for recovery of 3D phase, retardance and orientation.
source: Our method uses one polarization modulator, compared to six used by OI-DIC, and fewer images (5 × number of Z slices), compared to hundreds in ptychography-based method, for recovery of 3D phase, retardance and orientation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a comparison to prior methods.

claim: QLIPP measurements achieve diffraction-limited resolution and provide adequate time resolution for live-cell imaging.
source: Our measurements also achieve diffraction-limited resolution and provide adequate time resolution for live-cell imaging, as demonstrated by the 3D movie of U2OS cells (Figure 2, Figure 2—video 2, Figure 2—video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and demonstrated in Figure 2, Figure 2—video 2, and Figure 2—video 3.

claim: The modularity of the optical path and the availability of reconstruction software will facilitate adoption of QLIPP.
source: We anticipate that the modularity of the optical path and the availability of reconstruction software will facilitate adoption of QLIPP.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an anticipated outcome.

claim: QLIPP's approach of recovering phase from propagation of light reports the local phase variation rather than the absolute phase.
source: We note that our approach of recovering phase from propagation of light reports the local phase variation rather than the absolute phase.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a characteristic of the method.

claim: Local phase variation is less sensitive to low spatial frequency or large-scale variations in density.
source: Local phase variation is less sensitive to low spatial frequency or large-scale variations in density as can be seen from phase images n Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Recovering density at low spatial frequency requires a more elaborate optical path for creating interference with a reference beam and is more difficult to implement than QLIPP.
source: Recovering density at low spatial frequency requires a more elaborate optical path for creating interference with a reference beam and is more difficult to implement than QLIPP (Kim et al., 2018; Popescu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior work.

claim: Most biological processes can be visualized with the local density variation.
source: Nonetheless, most biological processes can be visualized with the local density variation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a justification for the method's approach.

claim: QLIPP uses partially coherent illumination, which improves spatial resolution, depth sectioning, and robustness to imperfections in the light path away from the focal plane.
source: Further, our method uses partially coherent illumination, that is, simultaneous illumination from multiple angles, which improves spatial resolution, depth sectioning, and robustness to imperfections in the light path away from the focal plane.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of the method.

claim: QLIPP belongs to the class of polarization-resolved imaging in which the specimen is illuminated in transmission.
source: QLIPP belongs to the class of polarization-resolved imaging in which the specimen is illuminated in transmission.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a classification of the method.

claim: PS-OCT is a label-free imaging method in which specimen is illuminated in reflection mode.
source: PS-OCT is a label-free imaging method in which specimen is illuminated in reflection mode.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a comparison to another method.

claim: PS-OCT has been used to measure round-trip retardance and diattenuation of diverse tissues, for example of brain tissue.
source: PS-OCT has been used to measure round-trip retardance and diattenuaton of diverse tissues, for example of brain tissue (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to prior work.

claim: Determination of the slow axis in reflection mode PS-OCT remains challenging due to the fact that light passes through the specimen in two directions.
source: But, determination of the slow axis in the reflection mode remains challenging due to the fact that light passes through the specimen in two directions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of PS-OCT.

claim: Fluorescence polarization imaging relies on rotationally constrained fluorescent probes.
source: Fluorescence polarization imaging relies on rotationally constrained fluorescent probes (DeMay et al., 2011; Mehta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior work.

claim: Fluorescence polarization measurements report the rotational diffusion and angular distribution of labeled molecules, which differs from QLIPP.
source: Fluorescence polarization measurements report the rotational diffusion and angular distribution of labeled molecules, which differs from QLIPP we have reported here.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a distinction from another method.

claim: QLIPP reports projection of the anisotropy onto the focal plane rather than 3D anisotropy.
source: We also note that, similar to other polarization-resolved imaging systems (Mehta et al., 2016), our approach reports projection of the anisotropy onto the focal plane rather than 3D anisotropy.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of the method, with a citation.

claim: Anisotropic structures such as axon bundles appear isotropic to the imaging system when they are aligned along the optical axis of the imaging path.
source: Anisotropic structures such as axon bundles, appear isotropic to the imaging system when they are aligned along the optical axis of the imaging path.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a consequence of the projection limitation.

claim: Methods for imaging 3D anisotropy with various models and systems are now in active development.
source: Methods for imaging 3D anisotropy with various models and systems (Oldenbourg, 2008; Spiesz et al., 2011; Axer et al., 2011c; Zilles et al., 2016; Schmitz et al., 2018a; Schmitz et al., 2018b; Yang et al., 2018; Tran and Oldenbourg, 2018) are now in active development.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to recent work.

claim: Recovering 3D anisotropy along with 3D density using forward models that account for diffraction effects in the propagation of polarized light would be an important area of research for the future.
source: Recovering 3D anisotropy along with 3D density using forward models that account for diffraction effects in the propagation of polarized light would be an important area of research for the future.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a future direction.

claim: Tractography algorithms developed for diffusion weighted-MRI measurements have been adapted to brain images from a lower-resolution polarization microscope.
source: Tractography algorithms developed for diffusion weighted-MRI measurements (Zhan et al., 2015) have been adapted to brain images from a lower-resolution polarization microscope (∼60 μm) (Axer et al., 2011c).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior work.

claim: Combining tractography algorithms with anisotropy measured at optical resolution will enable development of probabilistic models of connectivity.
source: We envision that combining tractography algorithms with anisotropy measured at optical resolution, which reports the orientation of ensemble of axons, will enable development of probabilistic models of connectivity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a future application.

claim: Multiple methods for tracing connectivity in the mouse brain at mesoscale have been developed but have not yet been extended to human brain.
source: Although multiple methods for tracing connectivity in the mouse brain at mesoscale (cellular level) have been developed (Ragan et al., 2012; Oh et al., 2014; Zeng, 2018), they have not yet been extended to human brain.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior work.

claim: Label-free measurement of myelination and axon tract orientation is possible with approximately 1.5 μm diffraction-limited resolution over the scale of whole fetal human brain sections.
source: Our data show that label-free measurement of myelination and axon tract orientation is possible with ∼1.5 μm diffraction-limited resolution over the scale of whole fetal human brain sections.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Further work in streamlining sample preparation, imaging, data curating, and model training would be required to apply QLIPP to large scale organs.
source: Further work in streamlining sample preparation, imaging, data curating, and model training would be required to apply QLIPP to large scale organs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a future direction.

claim: Multi-channel 2.5D deep learning models are designed for efficient analysis of multi-dimensional 3D data.
source: Our multi-channel 2.5D deep learning models are designed for efficient analysis of multi-dimensional 3D data.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a design principle.

claim: The 2.5D architecture provides comparable prediction accuracy at a lower computational cost than using 3D U-Net.
source: In contrast to earlier work on image translation that demonstrated 2D prediction (Christiansen et al., 2018; Rivenson et al., 2018a; Rivenson et al., 2018b), our 2.5D architecture is inspired by Han, 2017 and provides comparable prediction accuracy at a lower computational cost than using 3D U-Net.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior work.

claim: Pearson correlation coefficient in 3D for nuclei prediction from brightfield images is 0.87 vs. approximately 0.7 reported in Ounkomol et al., 2018.
source: Pearson correlation coefficient in 3D for nuclei prediction from brightfield images is 0.87 vs. ∼0.7 reported in Ounkomol et al., 2018.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a comparison to prior work.

claim: In Christiansen et al.'s 2D translation model, image translation was formulated as a pixel-wise classification task of 8-bit classes.
source: In comparison to Christiansen et al.'s 2D translation model (Christiansen et al., 2018) where the image translation was formulated as a pixel-wise classification task of 8-bit classes, our 2.5D model formulates the image translation as a regression task that allows prediction of much larger dynamic range of gray levels.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to prior work.

claim: The 2.5D model formulates image translation as a regression task that allows prediction of much larger dynamic range of gray levels.
source: In comparison to Christiansen et al.'s 2D translation model (Christiansen et al., 2018) where the image translation was formulated as a pixel-wise classification task of 8-bit classes, our 2.5D model formulates the image translation as a regression task that allows prediction of much larger dynamic range of gray levels.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of the current approach.

claim: Training a single model that predicts multiple structures requires increasing the model size with the trade-off of longer model training time.
source: While training a single model that predicts multiple structures seems appealing, this more complex task requires increasing the model size with the trade-off of longer model training time.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a consideration in model design.

claim: The modeling strategy to train one model to predict only one target allowed use of significantly smaller models that can fit into the memory of a single GPU for faster training.
source: Our modeling strategy to train one model to predict only one target allowed us to use significantly smaller models that can fit into the memory of a single GPU for faster training.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a design choice.

claim: The image quality metrics used to evaluate model performance depend on the accuracy of the prediction but also the noise in the target images.
source: The image quality metrics we use to evaluate the model performance depends on the accuracy of the prediction but also the noise in the target images.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of the evaluation approach.

claim: A more direct comparison of model performances on the same dataset would be useful in the future.
source: A more direct comparison of model performances on the same dataset would be useful in the future.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a future direction.

claim: The 2.5D network allows for application to image data that has only a few Z-slices without up- or down-sampling the data.
source: Further, the more flexible 2.5D network allows for application to image data that has only a few Z-slices without up- or down-sampling the data, making it useful for analysis of microscopic images that often has variable number of Z-slices.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of the 2.5D approach.

claim: The 2.5D network can be used for 3D segmentation.
source: Even though we focus on image translation in this work, the same 2.5D network can be used for 3D segmentation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a potential application.

claim: 3D segmentation using the 2.5D network bears additional advantages over 3D network because sparse annotation can be done on a subset of slices sampled from the 3D volume, while 3D network requires all the slices in the input volume to be annotated.
source: 3D segmentation using the 2.5D network bears additional advantages over 3D network, because sparse annotation can be done on a subset of slices sampled from the 3D volume, while 3D network requires all the slices in the input volume to be annotated.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of the 2.5D approach.

claim: The flexibility of sparse annotation allows for better sampling of structural variation in the data with the same effort on manual annotation.
source: The flexibility of sparse annotation allows for better sampling of structural variation in the data with the same effort on manual annotation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an advantage of sparse annotation.

claim: A common shortfall of machine learning approaches is that they tend not to generalize well.
source: A common shortfall of machine learning approaches is that they tend not to generalize well.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a known limitation of machine learning.

claim: The data normalization and training process leads to models of myelination that generalize to two developmental time points.
source: We have shown that our data normalization and training process leads to models of myelination that generalize to two developmental time points.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a finding of the work.

claim: In contrast to reconstruction using physical models, the errors or artifacts in the prediction by machine learning models are highly dependent on the quality of training data and their similarity to the new input data.
source: In contrast to reconstruction using physical models, the errors or artifacts in the prediction by machine learning models are highly dependant on the quality of training data and their similarity to the new input data.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a characteristic of machine learning approaches.

claim: Prediction errors made by machine learning models are difficult to identify in the absence of ground truth.
source: Therefore, prediction errors made by the machine learning models are difficult to identify in the absence of ground truth.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of machine learning approaches.

claim: Extending image translation models to predict not just the value but also provide estimate of the confidence interval of output values is an important area of research.
source: Extending the image translation models such that they predict not just the value, but also provide estimate of the confidence interval of output values, is an important area of research.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a future direction.

claim: The reconstruction algorithms are available at https://github.com/mehta-lab/reconstruct-order.
source: Our reconstruction algorithms (https://github.com/mehta-lab/reconstruct-order) and computationally efficient U-Net variants (https://github.com/czbiohub/microDL) facilitate measurement and interpretation of physical properties of the specimens.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusion as a resource availability statement.

claim: The computationally efficient U-Net variants are available at https://github.com/czbiohub/microDL.
source: Our reconstruction algorithms (https://github.com/mehta-lab/reconstruct-order) and computationally efficient U-Net variants (https://github.com/czbiohub/microDL) facilitate measurement and interpretation of physical properties of the specimens.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusion as a resource availability statement.

claim: Joint measurement of phase, retardance, and orientation was reported with diffraction-limited spatial resolution in 3D dividing cells and in 2D brain tissue slices.
source: We reported joint measurement of phase, retardance, and orientation with diffraction-limited spatial resolution in 3D dividing cells and in 2D brain tissue slices.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Diverse biological structures were visualized: axon tracts and myelination in mouse and human brain slices, and multiple organelles in cells.
source: We demonstrated visualization of diverse biological structures: axon tracts and myelination in mouse and human brain slices, and multiple organelles in cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Accurate prediction of fluorescent images from density and anisotropy was demonstrated with multi-contrast 2.5D U-Net model.
source: We demonstrated accurate prediction of fluorescent images from density and anisotropy with multi-contrast 2.5D U-Net model.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Strategies for accurate prediction of myelination in centimeter-scale prenatal human brain tissue slices were demonstrated.
source: We demonstrated strategies for accurate prediction myelination in centimeter-scale prenatal human brain tissue slices.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Inconsistent labeling of human tissue can be rescued with quantitative label-free imaging and trained models.
source: We showed that inconsistent labeling of human tissue can be rescued with qualitative label-free imaging and trained models.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The approach will enable quantitative label-free analysis of architectural order at multiple spatial and temporal scales, particularly in live cells and clinically-relevant tissues.
source: We anticipate that our approach will enable quantitative label-free analysis of architectural order at multiple spatial and temporal scales, particularly in live cells and clinically-relevant tissues.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusion as an anticipated impact.
